title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 1: Giving
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first of the four methods in Dogen's "Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance," giving, and reads the passage that opens with "giving means non-greed." Nomon slows the text down phrase by phrase, studying greed and the urge to curry favor, such as needing a smile from a quiet audience. Next comes "give yourself to yourself and others to others," which Nomon links to Katagiri Roshi's "settle the self on the self." A gratitude-journal research list follows, then listeners share recent gifts: broccoli from a garden, a stranger's grocery bill, a dead brother's generator sent to Haiti. Nomon closes with a bow to the dying Blanche Hartman.
topics: The Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance

sentences.text: **Nomon Tim Burnett:** Good evening everybody.
It's a really nice week you gather.
I was looking forward to thanking John for his wonderful talk last week on gratitude, but I guess he had to go home.

So, I was particularly appreciating, maybe you were too if you were here, that like John had a different assignment; he was going to do a talk about something else, but somehow gratitude was coming up, so he talked about that.
That's good, don't you think, to have an assignment and then do something else?
It's good for us.

And the last time I spoke a couple of weeks ago, I ended up just telling some stories about some of the work I've been doing in the mindfulness space, which wasn't exactly what I set out to do either.
Both of those were recorded, but it's not yet on the website, new or old, but it was on the recorder.
So, if you're technical and you're interested in learning how to upload dharma talks, see me later.
Probably shouldn't do that anymore because I don't get around to it.
My attention two weeks ago, and probably my attention a while ago, was to speak about a chapter from Dogen called the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance.
This is a lovely piece by Dogen.

It fits into our overall theme this year to study what it is to be a Bodhisattva—this term from Mahayana Buddhism, the kind of ideal way of being, a way of being that's oriented around awakening, orienting around supporting ourselves and others, and being, I was going to say the best we can be, but somebody else has that phrase.
But you know what I mean: devoting ourselves to waking up.
It's funny, last week I tried to study this text from Dogen.
I didn't have much time.
I felt rushed, and the text was like, you know, not that I'm trying to read something; it's just like little squiggles sort of floating around on the page.
It didn't make much sense.
This time I had a little more time and space, and somehow the text was very easy to read, very clear, very straightforward.
This is a nice text because we think of Dogen as fairly inaccessible, and we think of Zen in general as sort of tough and uncompromising.
I think you'll appreciate with me that this particular piece, Dogen emphasizes sweetness and kindness.
I'll read you the first section of the text.
*The Bodhisattva's four methods of guidance, wrote Master Dogen in 1243, are giving kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action.
The Bodhisattva's four methods of guidance are giving kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action.* And then he's going to have a section on each of these four things.
So, I thought tonight we'd focus on giving.
Dogen writes, giving means non-greed.
So, just kind of take this in, and we'll pick it apart a little bit in a minute.
Non-greed means to not to covet.
Not to covet means not to curry favor.
Even if you govern the four continents, you should always convey the authentic path with non-greed.
It is like giving away unneeded belongings to someone who doesn't know.
It's like offering flowers on a distant mountain to the Tathagata, the Buddha, or again offering treasures that you had in your former life to sentient beings.
Whether it is of teaching or of material, each gift has its value and is worth giving.
Even if the gift is not your own, there is no reason to abstain from giving.
The question is not whether the gift is valuable, but whether there is genuine merit.
*When you leave the way to the way, you attain the way.
When you leave the way to the way, you attain the way.
At the time of attaining the way, the way is always left to the way.
When treasure is left just as treasure, treasure becomes given.
You give yourself to yourself and others to others.
The power of causal relations of giving reaches to devas, human beings, even to enlightened sages.
When giving becomes actual, such causal relations are immediately formed.
The Buddha said, when a person who practices giving goes to an assembly, people take notice.
Know that the mind of such a person communicates subtly with others.
This being so, give even a phrase or a verse of the truth and it will become a wholesome seed for this and other lifetimes.
Give your valuables even a penny, even a blade of grass and it will become a wholesome root for this and other lifetimes.
The truth can turn into valuables, valuables can turn into the truth.
This is all because the giver is willing.*
Let's slow it down a little bit.
Dogen writes, giving means non-greed, non-greed.
Non-greed means not to covet.
Not to covet means not to curry favor.
So, what is he talking about?
Non-greed.
We could find out by noticing what greed is.
I think we all know what greed feels like, right?
To actually notice greed, to explore greed, to be interested in greed, and from that platform to look in the other direction, to look under, to look beyond, to look above, to look below.
What could be non-greed?
What could be not coveting?
Not currying favor?
I think the Sangha is, as always, a great laboratory, a great place to study giving and greed and non-greed.
This point he makes about currying favor is interesting because we can notice that here and in other parts of our life.
You can notice that desire for validation from someone, from a peer, from a teacher, from a newer student than us.
Maybe there's some way that we maneuver our body or our speech or our expression on our face to seek favor, to seek some kind of validation.
Sometimes that's okay; we are relative beings, right?
We have emotional needs and we need validation.
Where it goes sideways is when we seek validation without knowing that that's what we're doing.
We think we're trying to explain something.
We think we're trying to help somebody out.
We think we're just trying to get this right, but actually we're trying to manipulate somebody and seek validation.
Sometimes when I'm speaking to a group of people, which lately I'm doing a lot, and I'm getting like no obvious response.
You've all given presentations one way or the other in your life at some point.
Do you know that?
You're talking away, and you kind of look out there, and it's just like blank.
So sometimes I realize, "Well, I need some validation," just to do my job well.
I need some sense that I'm speaking a language that these people understand and that something's making, communicating something.
But then also I notice emotionally in this moment I actually need some support.
So I'll ask, "Is this making sense?
Is this kind of what you came to the talk for or the class for today?"
And some of them will smile and give me a nice little expression or say something.
I'll actually say, "Sometimes, thank you.
I was actually realizing I needed some emotional validation just then.
I was really kind of you to give that to me."
I hope that the class will also be valuable to you, but that helped me.
So, I think it's okay.
Dogen says giving is not seeking, not currying favor.
We can curry favor in a way that's actually giving if we know what we're doing and we're straightforward about it.
When we do it the other way, we can study that.
We can go home and sit down in the car and say, "Oh my gosh, you know, I was so manipulative just then.
I was really trying to get something from somebody with all kinds of justifications."
To understand giving and non-greed, I think we need to study greed.
To understand not currying favor, we need to curry favor.
If we do this with more awareness and light, it's transmuted into something beneficial, and we all grow and learn.
What I always say is great about the Sangha is—who really cares anyway, you know what I mean?
If these particular people like us or if we ring the bells the right way.
It's wonderful having different people ringing the bells and whacking on things.
The setup is such that we'll never do that quite right.
So, why are you doing that?
Are you seeking favor?
Do you want some validation?
"Good job.
You did do a good job."
And you made mistakes, and that's always true.
It goes on to say, it's like giving away unneeded belongings to someone you don't know.
It's like offering flowers blooming on a distant mountain to the Buddha.
It's like offering treasures that you had in your former life to sentient beings.
How would you even do this?
Whether you're giving teaching or material, each gift has its value and is worth giving.
Even if the gift is not your own, there's no reason to abstain from giving.
The question is not whether the gift is valuable, but whether there's merit.
In other words, don't let our narrow views about who we are and what we have and what the other person is or isn't hamper us.
Don't let our narrow, habitual, conditioned thinking limit our generosity.
Our giving can be beyond any idea of what we think we have or what we think the other person does or doesn't have.
The giving can have a power and a spirit that's beyond our sort of limited views of space and time, and that every gift has its value.
It's not so much whether it's like a good thing, but whether there's merit here.

By merit, what he's talking about is something we've been studying lately in our teacher's group from the Diamond Sutra: that for a gift to really have merit, you need to really let go of your idea of separation, of your idea that I'm over here like a good person or a bad person, whatever I think at this moment, and you're over there and you need this thing that I'm going to give you.
But that's really a limited view.
The merit is when we drop all that and we just give.
We just are just generous.
How can we do this?
How can we be giving beyond any idea of what's practical, what's real, what's unreal, what's valuable, what's not valuable?
Can we just give?
Can we just be giving?
Can we just practice non-greed?
He goes on, *when you leave the way to the way, this is practice instruction now, when you leave the way to the way, you attain the way.
At the time of attaining the way, the way is always left to the way.
When treasure is left just as treasure, treasure becomes giving.
You give yourself to yourself and others to others.
The power of the causal relations of giving reaches to Devas, human beings and enlightened sages.
When giving becomes actual, such causal relations are immediately formed.*
This is reminding us that you don't do it.

This is a great medicine for our idea that I'm over here trying to do the way, trying to do my practice, trying to do my life, and that I'm some sort of little actor in this play and I just need to get good at this and then I'll get it right.
He's saying no, settle it down.
The way for the way, the way unfolds, is leading it along, is letting it go, is dropping all that.
When you leave the way to the way, you attain the way.
There's something bigger than me, bigger than you.
Abandon all hope ye who enter here.
Dante didn't really mean it like Dogen, I don't think, but maybe he did, who knows.

But the beauty of surrender, as opposed to the tragedy of losing hope, the beauty of letting go of hope, because there's nothing but hope that the way will take care of ourself and take care of us and when we leave things be, they blossom.
That's blatantly one of my biggest goals in life.
I don't know if I'll ever be any good at this, and obviously Dogen says I won't be, because there's no me to do it.
But one of my biggest goals in life lately is, could I just leave more things alone?
Why do I keep messing with things?
Stirring things up?
Why can't I just appreciate things a little more and leave them a little more alone?
We'll see; I'm probably just it's my karma to mess with things.
The ultimate gift is mentioned here by Dogen, though: give yourself to yourself and others to others.
This is the biggest gift we can give—just give ourselves to ourselves.
Katagiri Roshi used to say that the way to do zazen was to settle the self on the self, settle the self on the self and let the life flower bloom.
Let your life flower bloom.
I remember he said, "Be your your."
So Dogen says the same: give yourself to yourself and others to others.
Obviously, we can't do this in the conventional way of giving.
How can I give others to others?
But when I give myself to myself, others give themselves to others.
When giving becomes actual, such causal relations are immediately formed, or another way of saying that things are complete.
The quality of things seems like not quite right, not quite done.
I always have more to do.
There's a spirit of practice here that allows the doneness to emerge.
It allows it to become apparent because it was already there.
There's a kind of completion that we can't find by taking, improving, or manipulating—a kind of completion that's just all about giving.
We'll do a little more and we'll do a reflection on our own giving practice.
This text is so interesting, isn't it?
On the one hand, I've gone back and forth.
A little moment there yesterday I was studying this, and it's like, "Oh, it's so clear."
And now I'm like, "Huh, what's he saying?"
Maybe you're bouncing back and forth too.
That's part of Dogen's genius, to kind of work with our limited view in that way with his language.
Dogen goes on, *The Buddha said, when a person who practices giving goes to an assembly, people take notice.
That's true enough, right?
Somebody who's really giving, you notice, you notice.
You notice their spirit, you notice their love.
And know that the mind of such a person communicates subtly with others.
This being so, give even a phrase or a verse of the truth and it will be a*
Wholesome seed for this and other lifetimes.
Give your valuables even a penny or a blade of grass, and it will be a wholesome root for this and other lifetimes.
The truth can turn into valuables; valuables can turn into the truth.
This is all because the giver is willing, is willing.
That's how he ends that section.
So, are we willing?
Are we actually truly willing to give?
Cultivating a giving mindset is really powerful.
He's saying, and this is pretty clear, right?
He's saying cultivating a giving mindset changes everything.
Things are communicated and expressed and connected.
Good things happen.
He makes a point, a cut here, and a couple of other times, don't be too hung up on what we're giving.
Like, "Oh, this isn't a good enough gift," or "I need to get something better for her," or "Oh, I forgot the card," or "Oh my god, it's a terrible card anyway."
We get so hung up on giving the right thing and giving it in the right way at the right time.
So, just give a blade of grass, just give a seed, just give a penny, but give it in this way, this whole connected way.
And that way we can practice with our stinginess and our unwillingness to give and transmute it, transform it into a willing generosity by just practicing giving.
Like, this is a practice.
This isn't like if I just study the right stuff and think about this right and do a whole hell of a lot of meditation, I will some magic moment be like, poof, a giving person.
I didn't use to be a giving person, and now I'm a giving person.
No, it's not what he's saying.
He's saying we're already a giving person, and we need to practice.
And it's great that John talked about gratitude because practicing gratitude is closely connected to practicing giving.
I was just reading that there have been scientific studies on the benefits of keeping a gratitude journal.
John was talking about kind of doing a sort of internal gratitude journal, but this is a suggestion to get a little notebook and put it by your nightstand and about three times a week.
The research suggests that doing this every day is less effective than about three times a week.
It comes across as a little too rote, I guess, who does this every day?
A little forced, like, "I gotta do my gratitude journal."
Do it three times a week.
And they've figured out what you should do.
You want to know?
One, be as specific as possible.
So not just some general thing, like, "I'm grateful I'm alive."
Why are you grateful?
For example, "I'm grateful that my co-workers brought me soup when I was sick on Tuesday."
Be specific.
That's better than, "I'm grateful for my co-workers."
Two, go for depth over breadth.
Go for detail.
What are you grateful for, really?
Three, get personal.
Focus on the people to whom you're grateful.
This has more impact than focusing on overall things that you're grateful for.
Four is interesting.
These are gratitude practices.
Writing down about gratitude will help our giving.
Try subtraction, not just addition.
Consider what your life would be like without certain people or things, rather than just tallying up the good stuff.
Be grateful for the negative outcomes you've avoided, prevented, or turned into something positive.
Try not to take the good fortune for granted.
Five, here's the connection.
See good things as gifts.
Thinking of the good things in your life as gifts that you have been given guards against taking them for granted.
Relish and savor the gifts you received.
Six, savor surprises.
That's good, huh?
Savor surprises.
Try to record events that were unexpected or surprising, as they tend to elicit stronger levels of gratitude.
Seven, revise if you repeat.
You find yourself, "I can only think of one thing I'm grateful for, so I'm just gonna write that down every time."
So try to find some subtle differences and details that are different each time.
Writing about some of the same people and things is okay, but zero in on a different detail that you're grateful for.
Eight, write regularly.
Whether you write every other day or once a week, commit to a regular time to journal your gratitude and honor that commitment.
But, number nine, don't overdo it.
Evidence is what I was saying.
Evidence suggests that writing occasionally, one to three times per week, is more beneficial than daily journaling.
This might be because we adapt to positive events and can soon become numb to them.
So we habituate to anything.
That's why it helps to savor surprises.
This is contemporary science from the Greater Good Science Foundation.
I read that they did a random controlled study of this.

Some people did the gratitude journal, some people did something else, and the people who did the gratitude journal experienced more gratitude, more positive moods, more optimism about the future, and slept better.
So this definitely puts us in a better space for practicing giving, right?
I mean, that's a good place to stop with Master Dogen.
We'll continue next time.
So, let's take a little minute now and contemplate our own conduct and see if we can focus our laser-like attention not on the negative, which we're so good at, but on the positive.
Maybe close your eyes if you don't mind and just kind of reflect back over today, for instance, or maybe other days recently.
Was there a time recently when you practiced giving, when you gave anything?
Doesn't have to be a big thing, right?
A plate of grass.
When you were generous, when you were kind, when you gave somebody the benefit of a doubt or material stuff or helpful suggestion or something.
Was there a specific time recently that you were giving?
That giving manifested itself through you?
It's always exactly something we deliberately do; it just happens.
And we won't go all the way around, like John did that, that was nice, but we don't want to put everybody in the spot.
If anyone can think of a time that you were giving, would you be willing to say a few words about it?
**Participant:** Yeah.
Excellent.
I have a garden, and it's coming into fruition now, and I gave a friend the first crop of broccoli florets and the first crop of baby bok choy.
Delicious.
It's a tangible giving.
Other giving.
Finding ways to give.
My husband and I have been finding ways to give each other time.
Time.
Really nice.

With a child, and we have a travel trailer on our property that someone lives into, and I was just really feeling so grateful last night for just that kind of time of coming home from work and the transition my child goes through during that time.
And just how Molly just stepped in and just took her for a walk so that we could have time together, and that was just really grateful.
You try to give each other time, but then Molly gave both of you time.
Yeah.
It was really nice.
Surprising.
Surprising.
Thank you.
**Participant:** Other stories of giving?
This afternoon my neighbor came over with her seven-year-old girl.
I got her to ask for a donation to the school, which I gave them, and we were talking about the daughter playing the piano.
So she plays, "Oh, did Julie, I think she plays on the piano, so I have a little keyboard."
So she sat down and played it beautifully.
And so when she got through, I said that was wonderful, and I see you understand fortissimo and fortissimo.
Yes.
And her mother said she didn't have anything, but it was really sweet.
Yeah.
The gift of giving a very specific.
Yeah.
That's lovely.
Fortissimo.
Darling child.
Yeah.
**Participant:** I'll tell this.
About three weeks ago, there was this young woman with two small children in front of me in the grocery store line, and she tried about three different cards and none of them worked.
And I could see the amount on the screen, and it wasn't a whole lot of money; it was about twenty-five dollars.
And I just told the clerk that I'd get it.
And yes, it felt good to do that, I guess.
And I don't know, it was just such a direct response.
I mean, it was no thinking about it at all.
That's a lovely example of exactly what Dogen was speaking about—just giving.
**Participant:** We had a going away party for a co-worker today, and I did most of the light work for fitting a gift in the card and putting it up and organizing the party together.
And then I gave away the giving.
I said, "Okay, you give her the card."
That's awesome.
Giving the giving.
Giving the giving.
Yeah.
Dogen should have had a line in there: "Give the giving away."
One more.
My brother died a few months ago, and we took a trip to Florida two weeks ago to clean his house out.
And it had the prospect of being a very exhausting and potentially complicated experience.
And we connected up with the local hospice who takes belongings, nice things for their thrift shop.
But beyond that, they introduced us to this man from Haiti who goes after them and takes things that people don't want and puts them on a container and ships them to Haiti.
So we had this wonderful relationship with him where we just said, "Here, do you want this?
Do you want this?"
We went into the tool shed.
There was a big generator, and his eyes just have it.
It was a wonderful time for all of us.
Your brother's generator went to Haiti.
It went into it with some priming that this might be really hard.
Thank you all for those reports.
Let's just keep experimenting with giving and gratitude.
And a little later we'll explore what Dogen means by kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action.
The last one is very interesting: identity action.
That's when he gets into full emptiness mode for us.
A few sangha reports before we close.
Chris Burkhart is healing and doing better.
If you don't know what happened, I'll tell you the story in brief.
She was practicing giving.
She was over on Salt Spring Island.
Hannah, you were there, I imagine, trying to help.
There's a lovely Zen group on Salt Spring Island, which is also where Hannah practices.
Peter Lovett is a teacher, and they have several people sewing the raka su to prepare for the Jukai ceremony, which we'll hopefully have one here in the fall too.
And Chris was there to do that giving away her weekend.
And one of the sangha members had a dog, and they were playing around with the dog and throwing the ball for the dog or something.
And somehow this dog charging after the ball just hit the back of Chris's legs in exactly the wrong way.
So that Chris just went flying.
And not just kind of knocked over, but end over end landed straight on top of her head.
Just somehow in a moment it was upside down on her head.
So she had a serious concussion.
And so she's gotten a lot of support and a lot of help and she's been really doing her best to follow the doctor's advice to rest and not talk or read or email.
And we caught her emailing the other day and chewed her out, but she's doing better.
Feels like she's healing.
And I don't know if you would know the other person I'm thinking of is Blanche Hartman, who's an early teacher of mine at San Francisco Zen Center, senior teacher there.
Blanche came to San Francisco Zen Center sometime around mid to late sixties, I think.
Studied with Suzuki Roshi in her late forties when she started.
And anyway, she's in her late eighties and has been going on pretty much fine, but suddenly, I don't remember the medical details, but suddenly came down with something.
Her husband died five, eight years ago, and she's ready to die, I think.
So she went into hospice yesterday.
So I haven't seen her that much in quite a while, but she and her husband Lou lived at Greenville's Farm when I first did residential training in nineteen eighty-six and seven.
And all I remember about her was that they have this practice there of stopping to bow to each other and the pathways when you're walking around the place.
And it's kind of a place where you go outside a lot between buildings as you pass people and the pathways.
And instead of trying to combat the rush, rush, rush, rush, and meet each other in a way that's quiet, the forum is you just stop and you bow to each other.
Which we do at sesshin.
When we go to the residential sesshin, we practice that way.
And anyway, I was like twenty, twenty-one, and feel like I didn't know what the hell was going on and trying to figure this thing out.
And I remember whenever I would pass Blanche, she would really stop and she would really do a deep bow, and really bow, you know, and then continue on her way.
And that stayed with me for thirty-five years now.
A bow.
So anyway, I just want to bow to Blanche Hartman and hope that her passing is peaceful.
And a lot of people will miss her, and I hope they can all let her go.
Give her the space to do what she needs to do.
And then Hannah mentioned her brother, and there are many other cards on the altar right now.
Many people seem like they're dying.
So, let's appreciate the biggest gift that we've been given, which Dogen talks about a little bit later: the gift of our body.
He says, let me just read you that one part.
Excuse me for going over, but it seems germane.
*If you study giving closely you see that to accept a body and to give up the body are both giving.
To accept a body and to give up a body are both giving.*
So, let's contemplate that little phrase of Dogen as we look at our own giving next weeks.
Thanks very much.
